html:
A work of mathematical astronomy written in Sanskrit verse by Brahmagupta in 628, at Bhillamala (modern Bhinmal) in Rajasthan. It is the first text known to treat zero as a number in its own right and to give rules for working with negative numbers.

Brahmagupta was about 30 when he wrote it. Most of its 24 chapters deal with astronomy: the motions of the planets, eclipses, and the calendar. He argued against earlier astronomers, including Aryabhata. Two chapters are pure mathematics, and those made it famous.

What it contains:

  • Rules for zero: a number minus itself is zero, and a number plus zero stays the same. He called positive numbers "fortunes" and negative ones "debts", and gave rules such as: a debt times a debt is a fortune. His rule that zero divided by zero is zero is now considered wrong.
  • A clear general method for solving quadratic equations.
  • Methods for whole-number solutions of equations of the type later called Pell's equation.
  • A formula for the area of a four-sided figure drawn inside a circle.

It was written without symbols, entirely in verse, to be memorised.

Around 770 an Indian astronomer brought it to the Abbasid court, and it was translated into Arabic in Baghdad. With the Indian numerals, its methods fed the work of al-Khwarizmi and passed, much later, to Europe through Fibonacci. The Gwalior inscription of 876 shows zero written as a round symbol in India.
